To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Late Bathonian - Early Oxfordian dinocyst assemblages are more similar to each other than the older Late Bathonian - Middle Callovian assembalges and that there is a decreasing similarity from north to south.

the dispersity of dinoflagallate cyst diversity increased from Late Bathonian through Early Oxfordian time, and the Simpson Coefficient of similarity between the dinoflalgellate cyst assembages decreased from Late Bathonian-Mid Callovian through Late Callovian to Early Oxfordian time.

the dinoflagellsate assemblages of the Late Bathonian-Oxfordian are profoundly different between Arctic and Mediterranean regions, but that they show a mixing of elements from the Arctic and Tethyan regions within the NW European region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biogeography of the dinoflalgellate cysts in the Late Bathonian-Oxfordian (Late Jurassic) of the Arctic, NW European and circum-Meditarranean regions.
the biogeography of the dinoflaegellate cysts in Arctic, NW Europe, and the circum-Mediterraneian regions during Late Bathonian to Oxfordia time.
the biogeographical and palaeoecological aspects of the Late Bathonian- Early Oxfordian dinocyst assemblages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dinoflagelate cysts show a similar biogeographic pattern to the ammonites.
the Late Bathonian- Early Oxfordian dinocyst assemblages are characterized by a gradual decrease in provinciality and an increase in dispersity of dinocysts.
the dinoflagallates are a good tool for biostratigraphy and that their distribution patterns are useful in paleogeographic reconstructions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dinoflagellete cyst assemblages in general appear to be more sensitive to the environmental changes than the ammonites, and that the distribution of dinoflagelletes is more sensitive to the changes in the sea-level than the distribution of the ammonites.
the distribution of dinoflagelate cyst assemblage types in the Late Bathonian-earliest Oxfordian interval is similar to that observed in older middle Jurassic time.
the dinoflagelates show a similar biogeographic pattern as the other marine organisms during Late Jurassic times.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of dinoflagelates can be used as an indicator of the presence or absence of barriers to dispersal.
the dinoflagelletes are a good tool for understanding the paleobiogeography of the Middle Jurassic.
the Late Jurassic was a time of great faunal mixing and that this mixing was reflected in the marine dinoflagellite floras.
